title: Rules that fade
scenario: A bookshop runs a support assistant on the OpenAI API. The developer instructions tell it to answer only about orders and shipping, in short replies. Turn 1 follows the rules. From turn 2 the assistant writes long essays on any topic. The team also wants to run the same assistant on the Claude API next quarter. You review the request code (exhibit).

questions.prompt: Why does the assistant stop following the rules from turn 2?

options.text: instructions apply only to the current request; earlier ones are not carried over.
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI text generation guide says exactly this. The rules were sent on turn 1 only.

options.text: The model forgets instructions after one turn on purpose, to save tokens and keep the cost down.
options.explanation: Nothing is forgotten on purpose. The rules were simply not part of the turn 2 request.

options.text: The user overrode the rules, because user messages rank above developer instructions in the OpenAI docs.
options.explanation: OpenAI documents the opposite order: developer instructions are prioritized ahead of user messages.

options.text: `instructions` are cached server-side for 60 seconds only, and turn 2 came too late to reuse them.
options.explanation: There is no such cache. `instructions` apply only to the request that carries them.

options.text: Send the same instructions with every request, from one place in the code.
options.explanation: Right. The API is stateless, so the system rules belong in every request. One shared constant keeps them consistent.

options.text: Paste the rules into the first user message instead.
options.explanation: That moves developer rules into the user channel, which ranks below developer instructions. Keep the channels apart.

options.text: Ask users to repeat 'only orders and shipping' in their questions.
options.explanation: Users should not carry your system's rules. Your app owns the instructions.

options.text: Store the instructions as a reusable prompt object in the vendor dashboard.
options.explanation: OpenAI is deprecating reusable prompt objects and advises keeping production prompts in your application code.

questions.prompt: Next quarter the same assistant runs on the Claude API. Where do the instructions go?

options.text: In the top-level system field of each Messages API request.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs say to use the top-level system field for instructions that apply from the start.

options.text: As the first entry of messages, with role system.
options.explanation: The Claude docs say a system message cannot be the first entry in messages. Use the top-level field.
developer is an OpenAI role. Claude uses the top-level system field.

options.text: Nowhere. Claude models do not take developer instructions at all.
options.explanation: They do, through the system field. The Claude docs show a role set there.

questions.prompt: The rule 'Keep replies under 80 words' is often ignored. Which rewrite follows the vendor guidance best?

options.text: Add the reason: 'Replies appear in a small chat bubble, so keep them under 80 words.'
options.explanation: Right. The Claude prompting guide says giving the motivation behind an instruction helps the model understand the goal.

options.text: Write it in capitals: 'NEVER WRITE MORE THAN 80 WORDS!!!' so the model sees it is urgent.
options.explanation: Shouting adds no information. The guide's own example shows a plain rule with its reason works better than a bare 'NEVER'.

options.text: Remove the rule and trim long replies in the UI after the model has written them.
options.explanation: Cutting text in the UI breaks sentences and still pays for the long output.

options.text: Move the rule to the end of every user message.
options.explanation: That mixes developer rules into user input. Keep rules in the developer channel and explain them.
